lessons.title: The Trap of Pseudo-Productivity
lessons.key_idea: Because knowledge work never defined productivity, we treat looking busy as a stand-in for real accomplishment, and that is burning us out.

lessons.title: Why Busyness Feels Like Progress
lessons.key_idea: Knowledge workers lost the clear measures of factory work, so emails, meetings and fast replies became the default signal of value.

lessons.title: Do Fewer Things
lessons.key_idea: Every project brings an overhead tax of coordination and communication, so taking on fewer commitments lets each one move faster and better.

lessons.title: Contain the Small Stuff
lessons.key_idea: Limit missions, projects and daily tasks, and use systems that pull in new work only when you have capacity, instead of letting requests pile on.

lessons.title: Work at a Natural Pace
lessons.key_idea: Many great thinkers of the past worked slowly over years, so set longer timelines and avoid making every day an urgent sprint.

lessons.title: Let Your Work Have Seasons
lessons.key_idea: Like farmers, alternate periods of intense effort with lighter stretches, instead of running at full speed all year.

lessons.title: Obsess Over Quality
lessons.key_idea: Caring deeply about the quality of your work ties the three principles together, because excellent work earns the freedom to slow down.

plan.title: Slow Productivity
plan.author: Cal Newport
plan.confidence_note: I know the book's core argument and its three principles well, but I am less certain of some finer anecdotal details, so lessons stick to the main ideas.
plan.one_liner: Busyness isn't the same as good work. Do fewer things, slower and better, to accomplish more.
plan.summary: Cal Newport argues that modern knowledge work never settled on a real definition of productivity. Without one, people fell back on visible activity, like fast email replies, packed calendars and constant meetings, as a stand-in for real accomplishment. He calls this pseudo-productivity and says it drives the burnout so many professionals feel. As an alternative, he offers slow productivity, built on three principles. First, do fewer things, because every commitment carries hidden overhead that crowds out real progress. Second, work at a natural pace, on longer time horizons and with seasonal variation, the way many great thinkers of the past did. Third, obsess over quality, because work that is truly excellent earns the leverage to protect a calmer way of working. The result is a sustainable path to meaningful results without exhaustion.
